To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The parasite population in the mouse model is genetically highly diverse.
The parasite strain-specificity of protective immunity to malaria is determined by the parasite strain-specificity with which protective immunity is induced.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following: 1) The use of the P. chabaudi chabaudi model to study the development of immunity and its regulation.
(a) the identification of parasite antigens and their immunogenicity; (b) the characterization of immune responses to these antigens; and (c) the development of a vaccine for malaria.
the study of the immunology of malaria in the mouse and the application of these findings to the understanding of human disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the immune system in the mouse is able to recognize the parasite strain-specific antigens on the parasite-infected erythrocytes.
the immune system of a host is able to recognize a large number of different parasite antigens and to respond to each of them with an appropriate effector mechanism.
the parasite population is not clonal, and the parasite population size is not limited.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(i) the parasite has a limited repertoire of antigenic variants which are not randomly distributed in the parasite population but are clustered within the population, (ii) a single variant is able to induce protection against challenge by a homologous variant and to a limited extent against heterologous variants, (iii) the protective response to a single variant can be enhanced by immunisation with a second variant and (iv) the response to a single parasite antigen can be boosted by a second parasite antigen.
the induction of a protective response is a function of the parasite genotype and that the effector mechanism(s) are directed against the variant surface antigen.

(a) the parasite population can be divided into a limited number of antigenically distinct subpopulations, (b) each subpopulation is composed of a limited number of phenotypically distinct antigenic variants, and (c) the parasite population as a whole is composed of a very large number of distinct variants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a combination of serology and DNA technology can help us understand the specificity of the immune responses to malaria.
a single parasite strain can express a wide diversity of variant antigens.
the induction of protective immunity is not a simple process, but one that is complex and dependent on the interplay between parasite strain and host genotype.
